item.title: After Lockdown, Sea of Protesters Flows Through India’s Capital
item.description:
Thousands of opposition political party supporters marched along a busy thoroughfare in central Delhi to challenge sweeping revisions of the nation’s voter roll.

In a contrast to a week of lockdowns and detentions by the authorities, the demonstrators on Monday far outnumbered security forces stationed on the road. They stood atop orange buses, waving the flags of the opposition Indian National Congress party. Columns of police and other security officials, dressed in riot gear, watched.

The turnout signaled a show of strength for the long-beleaguered Congress party leader, Rahul Gandhi. He marched with a rambunctious crowd, at times flanked by his sister, Priyanka Gandhi Vadra. In an effort to portray a unified front against the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party, Mr. Gandhi was also joined by Neha Bora, a leftist student activist, along with regional politicians from North India.

Mr. Gandhi’s lawyer filed a petition on his behalf in the Supreme Court, calling for an inquiry into the proceedings of the election commission. Its chief, Gyanesh Kumar, has been the target of more than a week of protests across India, by youth groups, opposition politicians, and ordinary citizens who say the election commission’s revision of the voter roll is a politically motivated purge of critics of the ruling party. Since it began last summer, the revision has expunged over 130 million names.

Together, months of protests over a wide range of frustrations about poor education and a lack of job opportunities represent the biggest challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi in his 12 years in office.

The government’s tactics on Monday, allowing the march to proceed mostly unimpeded, were a stark contrast to the intense crackdown on protests over the course of the last week, when would-be demonstrators were grabbed and stuffed into police vans.

The crowd was so thick at Monday’s march that it could barely move. There were several moments when Mr. Gandhi was just pushed along through a sea of people.

In a news conference earlier, the opposition, who was detained in demonstrations in Delhi last week, vowed to continue to protest.

“We will do it today, they will stop us. We will do it tomorrow, they will stop us. We will do it the day after tomorrow. They will stop us,” he said. “Let them stop us.”

By evening, there was no sign of the mass detentions of recent days.

Rather, politicians from the B.J.P., the ruling party, fired back with political invective.

“Congress is a group of hooligans trying to spread chaos on the streets and oppose the system,” a B.J.P. minister, Shivraj Chouhan, said.

Anurag Thakur, a B.J.P. member of parliament, said: “Rahul Gandhi and the Congress Party’s motto is — if not in power, then spread anarchy. “

The march came as the government declared that protests can no longer be legally held inside the small area in central Delhi that is the seat of government power.

What had been the capital’s most popular protest site for decades — an 18th-century monument called Jantar Mantar that sits less than a mile from India’s Parliament — would no longer be used for demonstrations, the government said in its “guidelines for holding protests or demonstrations in Delhi.”

The government said permission for protests can only be sought at three other sites: one about 3 miles from parliament, another further away in the east of the city, and the third to the north. Critics said the change effectively sidelines dissent, moving it away from the halls of power.

“Peaceful assembly & protest is a fundamental right of people,” Prashant Bhushan, a lawyer and civil rights activist, said in a social media post. “The govt cannot confine to ‘Designated sites.’”

Removing Jantar Mantar as a protest site came two days after the youth movement known as the Cockroach Janta Party had called for nationwide protests to be held there on Saturday. The Delhi police denied permission for the protest and took extraordinary measures to prevent people from assembling, canceling trains to the capital, closing metro stations and shutting off the internet in the city center.

Jantar Mantar, distinguished by its ocher-colored sundial, is a relatively small venue with two entrance and exit gates and the government had begun looking for alternate sites for sanctioned protests several years ago. The Supreme Court on Saturday recommended that the government look for alternate protest sites.

Anjani Anand, 29, came to the march Monday afternoon on Barakhamba Road, less than a mile away from Jantar Mantar, with a few friends. “I think people feel safer to come out onto the streets,” she said.

“There’s strength in numbers here,” said Shubhayan Sengupta, 30, who had joined her. He had been detained twice on Saturday and escaped both times. He didn’t want to be detained again, but he and his friends were prepared. They had the numbers of lawyers.

item.title: ‘There Are No Words’: Dozens Killed in Airstrikes Near Sudan-Egypt Border
item.description:
Dozens of gold workers in northern Sudan were killed over the weekend after warplanes bombed an open air mine near the Egyptian border, according to Sudanese rights groups, graphic video and eyewitnesses interviewed by The New York Times.

Footage from the aftermath of the bombing showed badly mutilated bodies of young men scattered amid sacks of mineral ore at a remote site in River Nile State, roughly 25 miles from Sudan’s border with Egypt.

“We were overcome with terror,” said Saif Eldin Adam, 26, a university student who worked at the mine for the past three months. Mr. Adam said he helped rescue the wounded and recover the dead after the strikes.

“There are no words for what we saw,” he said.

Emergency Lawyers, a rights group, estimated the death toll at 72. Two eyewitnesses said it was at least 65, with another 120 or more wounded.

The attack occurred hundreds of miles from the front lines of Sudan’s devastating civil war. Sudanese media reports and several rights groups blamed the strike on Egypt. Last June, miners accused Egyptian forces of carrying out a drone attack on another gold mine in the same region.

Sudan mines billions of dollars in gold every year, with the two warring sides using the profits to bankroll their fight. Sudan’s military has bombed mines controlled by its enemy, the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, in the far south of the country, in an effort to curtail a valuable source of finance.

The attack on Saturday was striking because it occurred in an army-controlled area largely untouched by fighting, and because the loudest accusations were directed at Egypt, a country that has been a staunch ally of Sudan’s military throughout the war.

In February, The Times revealed a covert Egyptian drone base that supported the Sudanese military’s war effort.

In a statement, Egypt’s military spokesman said its forces were in the third phase of “a major campaign to combat illegal gold prospecting in the Eastern Desert,” which came after leaflets were dropped to warn what he called “criminal elements.”

But the statement insisted that Egyptian forces had been acting inside their own borders, and not in Sudanese territory.

Sudan’s military avoided pointing fingers. On Monday the military chief, Gen. Abdul Fattah al-Burhan, announced an investigation into what he called a “painful incident.”

The bombing was notable in Sudan, even during an atrocity-laden conflict that has seen credible accusations of genocide, chemical weapons use, mass rape and starvation.

The targets of the strike appeared to be poor, largely young miners laboring in harsh conditions in a remote area. Graphic footage filmed in the aftermath of the strikes shows severely wounded civilians. Other videos filmed by miners show fighter jets flying over the area and munitions striking the ground.

“Just scatter, guys! Scatter!” one witness shouts as a plume of smoke rises from the mountain and a plane is heard flying overhead.

One of the men described to The Times how the strikes unfolded.

During a video call, Bahar Eldin Hassan said that warplanes and helicopters made several passes over the mine early on Saturday. From about 9 a.m., warplanes bombed the site at least three times over the course of an hour, he said.

About 35 people died in the first strike, he said, adding: “I cannot describe how terrible the scenes we saw were.”

Artisanal mining, where poor men dig for riches at informal mines, is booming across Africa. Soaring prices for gold, copper and other minerals have drawn workers across a wide belt of the continent. But artisanal mining is also notorious for dangers and human rights abuses, including child labor.

Mr. Adam, a student at Sudan University of Science and Technology, said he took shelter in a mining pit alongside a “terrified” young boy after the strikes. “He wanted to run away without knowing where he was going, but I managed to convince him to stay,” he said. “When we came out, the scene was horrific. I broke down crying.”

Footage appeared to show more than two dozen bodies wrapped in fabric following the strikes. In yet another video, a crowd is gathered outside a medical center where dozens of victims were reportedly taken, according a local Sudanese report.

Videos taken in the aftermath of the strikes showed what appeared to be Egyptian munitions. One video showed what looked to be an unexploded Egyptian NASR 400 bomb, according to Trevor Ball, a former U.S. Army explosive ordnance disposal technician who analyzed the footage for The Times.

In June, Egypt’s military said in a statement that it had begun a security campaign targeting criminal networks and what it described as illegal mining in southern Egypt, near the border with Sudan.

Its campaign included a Facebook video urging miners to leave the area before they were detained by the authorities.

Days later, several miners were killed on the Sudanese side of the border following an attack by Egypt’s military, according to The Sudan Tribune and witness accounts posted on social media. Some reports said the Egyptians distributed leaflets warning miners that they could be “considered a target for immediate attack” if they remained in the area.

The Times was unable to immediately verify the precise location of the attacks on Saturday, given the expansive mountainous area where the footage was filmed. The Times confirmed that the footage did not appear online before Saturday, and geographic features in the video matched other footage showing the aftermath of the strikes.

The scenes depicted were consistent with local reporting, and several of the videos were posted to the TikTok accounts of miners who work in the area.

“Those killed were like brothers to us,” said Mr. Adam. “ We worked together, we ate together, we sat around chatting together. That was our lives.”

Despite its dangers, gold mining has become an economic mainstay in Sudan during a war that has otherwise devastated the economy. Even after a bombing, some miners said they had little choice but to continue.

Mr. Hassan, who uses his earnings to support eight brothers and one sister, said he expected to be back at work soon.

Sanjana Varghese and James McManagan contributed reporting.

item.title: Macron Dreamed of Reviving France, but His Term Is Ending in Crisis
item.description:
As thousands of high school students took to the streets last week in a collective cry of youthful anger, President Emmanuel Macron of France traveled to a navy ship off the coast of Brittany. From the deck, he watched the firing of a new ballistic missile from a French nuclear-powered submarine.

It was a telling display of Mr. Macron’s priorities in a country where the president, by tradition, rises above the messy scrum of domestic politics. Mr. Macron left it to his prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, to try to reassure the French people that the government was handling the proliferating unrest.

It also reflected how Mr. Macron, after nearly a decade in power, has failed to solve the manifold problems afflicting France’s economy and welfare system — problems he promised to address when he was elected in 2017, at 39, as an ambitious reformer, and which have now coalesced into a systemic crisis.

“Remember, Macron published a book before the 2017 election, called ‘Révolution,’” said Jérôme Fourquet, a political analyst at the polling institute IFOP. “We told ourselves: he will relaunch the machine, he will lead a revolution.”

With just seven months before he leaves office, the president “hasn’t been able to bring about this revolution,” Mr. Fourquet said. Instead, the analyst said, he may be remembered as “the last captain of the boat.”

On Tuesday, thousands of students were set again to protest overcrowded classrooms, dilapidated school buildings and a shortage of teachers. The protests, now in their fourth week, added to the portrait of a country in disarray.

So dire are France’s fiscal problems that experts say the country may finally be forced to reckon with the foundering of its generous welfare state. Such a scenario could trigger painful cuts to benefits or even a default on France’s debt.

To be sure, many of these problems predated Mr. Macron. Some were exacerbated by events out of his control, like the coronavirus pandemic and wars in Iran and Ukraine, which fueled inflation and further busted the budget.

Still, critics say Mr. Macron failed to make a dent in France’s longstanding structural problems, either because of public blowback or his own political miscalculations. His legacy, then, is likely to be one of unfulfilled promise.

Mr. Macron’s office declined to comment.

A onetime investment banker who had served as economics minister, Mr. Macron came in promising to revitalize France’s economy by cutting taxes on businesses and high-income people, loosening labor laws and overhauling the pension system. This, he said, would nurture an entrepreneurial culture and make France attractive again to investors, which would reignite economic growth.

Mr. Macron accomplished the first two goals but not the third. He set off angry protests after pushing through an unpopular rise in France’s retirement age to 64 from 62, a move that economists say was critical to stemming the tide of red ink. After Mr. Macron lost his majority in the National Assembly, lawmakers bowed to popular sentiment, voting in 2025 to pause the change.

At the same time, Mr. Macron’s elimination of a tax on wealthy people earned him the unflattering sobriquet “president of the rich.” That became a political problem as rising prices created a cost-of-living squeeze. From 2018 to 2020, France was convulsed by the “Yellow Vest” protest movement, which began when people turned out to demonstrate against fuel prices and a litany of other grievances.

“We never had so many very rich people, and we have many people who can’t make ends meet,” said Jean-Yves Camus, a political scientist at the Jean Jaurès Foundation, a left-leaning think tank in Paris. “French society, which always aimed at being egalitarian, is going the American way.”

France, of course, remains starkly different to the United States when it comes to the size of the state. In 2025, public spending — on heath care, pensions, education, culture and other benefits — amounted to 57.3 percent of France’s total economic output. That is the second highest percentage in the European Union, after Finland’s, and more than 20 points higher than in the United States.

Total public debt is now projected to reach 120 percent of gross domestic product in 2027, the third-highest ratio after those of Greece and Italy.

Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and President Trump’s return to power in 2024, compounded France’s costs because it has had to spend more on its military — both to counter Russian threats and to rely less on America’s security umbrella.

Even critics credit Mr. Macron for leading calls for the continent to take on more responsibility for its security. His blueprint for “strategic autonomy” from the United States once seemed unrealistic, even grandiose. Given Mr. Trump’s disparagement of NATO, it now seems prescient.

“He has tried to build a global European vision,” said Gérard Araud, a former French ambassador to Washington, said of Mr. Macron, whom he has advised. “Whatever you think of it, he has been the voice of Europe.”

But Mr. Araud said that the qualities that had enabled Mr. Macron to stride the global stage have hurt him at home. His elite credentials and intellectual manner have made him seem out-of-touch in meat-and-potatoes France, he said.

“He’s the ultimate arugula president in a populist time,” said Mr. Araud, recalling an early episode in which Barack Obama, who some say shares a few of Mr. Macron’s highhanded traits, was tweaked for mentioning rarefied salad leaves in a meeting with farmers.

French voters have long since grown disillusioned with Mr. Macron. His approval rating stood at 15 percent, the lowest level since he took office, according to a poll last week by the polling firm, Ipsos. Mr. Macron’s eroding popularity has coincided with a skein of electoral setbacks, some of them self-inflicted.

After his party was badly beaten in European Parliament elections in 2024, the president called snap elections within France. The decision, which surprised his advisers, backfired, leaving his party with fewer seats in the national Parliament.

Mr. Macron found himself with little room for legislative maneuver as France’s fiscal situation continued to deteriorate. His push to overhaul the French state was by then a memory. The eruption of the Iran war drove up energy prices again, further clouding France’s economic picture.

Even in pushing for an end to the conflicts in Iran and Ukraine, Mr. Macron has found himself largely on the sidelines of negotiations dominated by the United States. One exception was when he recently negotiated a deal with Mr. Trump and other leaders to release 100 million barrels of stockpiled crude oil and diesel to ease prices that war has raised.

At home, Mr. Macron has cycled through prime ministers as the government has labored to pass a budget. The seemingly unending drama over France’s finances has deepened the doubts of investors about the country’s creditworthiness.

With yields on France’s bonds briefly crossing the dangerous threshold of 5 percent, there are fears that the country could tumble into a full-blown financial crisis. Investors are also alarmed by the prospect that the far-right leader Marine Le Pen has a plausible path to the presidency next spring.

Mr. Macron, who twice defeated Ms. Le Pen, has long presented himself as a bulwark against the far right. But his inability to turn his political movement into a self-sustaining centrist party, analysts said, has contributed to the withering of France’s political center, leaving the country vulnerable to a far-right takeover.

Alain Minc, a French businessman who was a close adviser to Mr. Macron before falling out with him midway through his tenure, said the president’s legacy could be divided neatly into halves.

Mr. Macron’s first term, during which he pushed through some significant changes, was “more than decent.” His second, Mr. Minc said, was a “drama,” culminating in the current crisis, which has prompted some to question whether France will need to be bailed out by the European Central Bank.

“His legacy will be dramatic,” Mr. Minc said, and not in a good way. “For France to need the support of the E.C.B. is the most humiliating position to be in.”

Giulia Imbert and Ségolène Le Stradic contributed reporting.

item.title: At Least 6 Injured in Stabbing in South Korea
item.description:
At least six people were injured after a man went on a stabbing rampage at a supermarket in Incheon, South Korea, on Tuesday, the police said.

The police said the attack took place at around 1:50 p.m. at a branch of Homeplus, a supermarket chain. The conditions of the victims were not immediately clear.

The suspect was in custody and his motive was being investigated, according to the Incheon Metropolitan Police. Video from local news media showed the authorities escorting a man outside the store.

Mass acts of violence are rare in South Korea. In 2023, a stabbing and car rampage near Seoul, the capital, killed one and injured 13 others. It came just weeks after another attack killed one and injured three others in central Seoul.

Tuesday’s attack was in Incheon, a city west of Seoul and the site of the country’s main international airport.

The store, as well as Homeplus’s corporate headquarters, did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

This is a developing story.

item.title: Nuremberg Airport in Germany Suspends Flights Over ‘Aviation Emergency’
item.description:
An airport in Nuremberg, Germany, said it had shut down operations on Tuesday because of an unspecified “aviation emergency” involving a flight from Corfu, Greece. The German police said it had determined there was “no danger” with the flight but did not provide details.

“Flight operations have been suspended for the time being,” the Albrecht Dürer Airport in Nuremberg said on its website. “More information will follow.”

The notice later added that Flight XR456 from Corfu to Nuremberg had “now landed safely,” but it was not immediately clear how that flight was connected to the alert.

The police department in Mittelfranken, which is responsible for the Nuremberg area, later said on social media: “On-site inspections have determined that there is no danger.”

The police statement referred to a regularly scheduled plane from Corfu that had landed in Nuremberg, but it did not specify an exact flight number.

Nuremberg’s airport is a regional hub that mostly services holiday destinations in southern Europe and Turkey. Last year the airport handled 4.5 million passengers, according to its own statistics.

This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

item.title: This Copper Mine Led to a Civil War. Can Reopening It Fund a New Nation?
item.description:
The years had covered the skeletal structures of the abandoned mine with rust, filling its shafts with sludge and debris several stories deep. Green leaves sprouted from crumbling industrial equipment. What was left of a water pump station was repurposed as a church, with steel beams for pews.

Four decades ago, the vast Panguna mine on Bougainville, an island on the eastern edge of Papua New Guinea, abruptly shut down. It closed after sabotage by residents irate that less than 2 percent of the wealth generated by the Australian-run copper and gold mine went to the local community, even though it obliterated whole villages and buried swaths of land downstream in mine waste.

That anger spiraled into a decade-long civil war in the island’s jungles, as a ragtag separatist militia held Papua New Guinea’s military at bay. “The Crisis,” as it is now known, left as many as 15,000 people dead and displaced a generation, while cementing Bougainville’s desires for independence.

Now, the dormant mine is whirring back to life, spurred by aspirations for the region to become the world’s newest country — and a growing appetite for copper. Its leader, President Ishmael Toroama, a former rebel commander, has pledged Bougainville will be governing itself by next year, its future funded by the mine.

Global demand for the estimated 5.3 million tons of copper buried in its depths has surged. But the rush of interest raises the question: Will its resources be extracted in a way that benefits the people of Bougainville, or will history repeat itself?

Late last year, the Autonomous Bougainville Government brought on a little-known Indian company, Lloyds Metals and Energy, as a partner in redeveloping the mine. Since then, heavy machinery has been careening along unpaved roads leading to the pit, while mining engineers and technicians from India have filled lodges in the nearby town of Arawa. Former combatants loyal to the president guard access to the mine, which Lloyds said in a statement should resume operations in early 2028.

The rapid progression has unnerved some landowners, observers and older Bougainvilleans who remember the descent into conflict and worry of renewed violence.

“If you’re walking fast, too fast, you have more chances of sliding over and probably you can even break your head,” said Dennis Kuiai, who fought alongside the president and is now a regional director in the Justice Department. “We should be taking time, making sure that we are doing things the right way.”

Lloyds said in the statement it was aware of the sensitivities.

“Panguna’s history makes careful consultation with landowners and communities essential,” the company said, adding that its aim was a project that “delivers lasting local benefits.”

Tensions briefly erupted this month, when 45 heavy vehicles bearing the Lloyds insignia were set on fire by saboteurs presumed to be local alluvial miners. Mr. Toroama called it an “isolated act of violence by individuals” and said work will “continue without delay.”

The geography around Panguna is defined by vestiges of the mine. Instead of referring to villages by name, people will say they live by the drainage tunnel, the water pump station, in the pit or on the upper, middle or lower tailings — large areas covered in mine waste.

In August, New York Times journalists spent several days in Bougainville, traveling to the bottom of the mine pit and throughout the area, speaking to residents and workers. In a sign of sensitivities, some workers accused journalists of spying for other would-be mine operators, and an agitated group of men who said they were former combatants briefly wrested away the photographer’s camera.

Philip Ken’s village, which was forced to relocate three times because of the mine, now sits by the pump station-turned-church. There, the psalm from Sunday’s service was scrawled on a chalkboard, and two statues of the Virgin Mary gazed out at the nave.

Born in 1970, two years before the mine opened, Mr. Ken only knows from stories what his home was like before — that wild pigs roamed, and the river teemed with fish. “My family was living downstream. Now it’s a desert,” said Mr. Ken, 56. He fought in the Bougainville Revolutionary Army in the conflict that lasted from 1988 to 1998. “I fought for my land, having heard what the mining had done.”

In the years since the mine was halted, people in his village and others have relied on panning for gold in the runoff. The tough but profitable work draws children as young as 10. Many use mercury because it binds to gold. The health effects are apparent in his community, where few live past 60, Mr. Ken said.

“You cannot see gray hairs in the tailings,” he said.

For the first time in decades, Lloyds is promising new jobs. Young women from Mr. Ken’s village are among 150 the company has started training to sew — but the wages pale in comparison with alluvial mining.

Whether Bougainville can be economically viable on its own has been a key question on its path to independence.

In a peace agreement signed in 2001, Papua New Guinea and Bougainville’s leaders agreed that the territory would be run autonomously, and that a referendum would be held to determine its political future. In 2019, that vote was finally held, and Bougainvilleans’ wishes were resounding: 98 percent wanted independence. At the same time, lawmakers in Papua New Guinea have questioned whether Bougainville can sustain itself economically.

Delivering independence has fallen to Mr. Toroama, the president, whose left arm was maimed by a grenade in the crisis. He has referred to the mine as the “economic guarantor for Bougainville’s independence” saying Panguna will free Bougainville from dependence on Papua New Guinea, which still funds most of its budget.

Not everyone is convinced.

“The president thinks we get independence just by opening the mine,” said Michael Pariu, 77, chief of the Nasioi people, whose village is near the tunnel. The rush to reopen seemed to take precedence over other basic preparations, like governance, social services and education, he said.

Mr. Toroama did not respond to multiple requests for an interview.

In November, Mr. Toroama surprised Bougainvilleans by signing a memorandum of understanding with Lloyds Metals, which operates iron ore mines in India but had no track record of developing or operating mines internationally. Mr. Toroama rejected a proposal to partner with CMOC, a major Chinese miner and one of the world’s top copper producers.

“If Lloyds Metals and Energy Limited truly respects Bougainville’s past, then the first test will be transparency, accountability, and a clear demonstration of how this partnership will uplift our people — not just extract our resources,” one resident, Walter Magut Buk, wrote in a Facebook comment on the day of the announcement.

The lack of transparency over the selection process has prompted concern about the company and its relationship to Mr. Toroama.

In February, John Momis, who served as president from 2010-2020, issued a statement questioning whether Lloyds had the ability to raise the billions necessary to reopen the mine.

He also criticized “a range of benefits and inducements” the company had provided Mr. Toroama, including flying his wife to India for “serious and expensive medical assistance.” In a community interwoven with family connections, it is widely known that the president’s wife was taken to India for a kidney transplant — a type of lifesaving care few in Bougainville have access to.

Lloyds said it provided assistance to Betty Toroama for “humanitarian” reasons.

“We reject the suggestion that our assistance was intended to influence the selection of a development partner for Panguna,” the company said.

By mid-August, signs of Lloyds’ ramp-up of operations were apparent throughout the Panguna area and in Arawa. Residents carried golf umbrellas bearing the Bougainville flag and the Lloyds logo, reinforcing the association between independence and the company. Rows of new heavy machinery sat in the nearby Loloho Port. Construction was in full swing at the site of a 100-bed hospital Lloyds had promised to build.

In a mine shaft inside the Panguna pit, workers said they had been shoveling away for a month at 40 years of accumulated sludge. One man said he was being paid minimum wage of 5 kina per an hour, about $1.12, and had not been given gloves or masks. He glanced over his shoulder, and stopped speaking when an Indian supervisor approached.

A former Lloyds employee, who asked not to be named because they have been threatened by former combatants, said the company did not sign employment contracts and made most payments in cash. The company said that although some early salaries may have been paid in cash, all current employees had contracts.

“We’d always be told, the president wants this done,” the former employee said. “We need to do this quickly, we want this yesterday.”

Lloyds promised that they can get the mine up and running faster than other companies, particularly Western ones, said Samson Kaissy, chairman of the landowners’ council.

“With Lloyds, they will never waste time. Once they talk, at the same time, they bring the funds,” he said.

The race to restart the mine complicates another hard-fought process: cleaning up the devastation left behind by the departure of Rio Tinto, the mine’s Australian former operator.

Theonila Roka Matbob was among 156 Bougainvilleans who filed a complaint against the mining giant in 2020, seeking remediation for environmental and human rights harms. Some of the most urgent work was getting underway just as Lloyds entered the picture, she said. Rio Tinto has said it is continuing to engage in efforts to address the mine’s impacts.

“We have a legacy to fix,” said Ms. Matbob, who filed the complaint with Australia’s Human Rights Law Center. She said she worried the hurried reopening was “jumping on the wagon on the way to more destruction.”

Ms. Matbob, 35, whose father was killed during the crisis, said her village had been rebuilding the community and rehabilitating their land. From 1972 to 1988, the mine was churning out 100,000 tons of waste rock daily, enough to fill a football field three stories high, deposited downstream.

On a rainy day in early August, in a bid to ease tensions, the government staged a “blood cleansing” ritual at the mine to release the land of its burdens. It said in a statement it wanted to dispel notions that former combatants were taking over mine operations by force.

Mr. Toroama, with an array of Lloyds umbrellas visible behind him, assured his people that everything was in service of Bougainville’s independence.

“This is it, the time is here with us,” he thundered, over the drumming of the downpour. “Together with Lloyds Metals, the work must progress.”

item.title: Pope Leo Prepares for Surgery to Remove Lung Nodule
item.description:
Pope Leo XIV will undergo surgery on Tuesday to remove a nodule from his lung, the Vatican said. It will be Leo’s first medical issue requiring hospitalization since he became the pontiff last year.

Leaving the Vatican on Tuesday morning, Leo waved through a rolled-down car window to a group of well-wishers that had gathered outside the Vatican walls.

He received a hero’s welcome when he arrived at the main entrance of the Policlinico A. Gemelli hospital, with dozens of people waving and cheering as the pontiff made his way inside.

“We’re with you,” one person called out from the crowd.

The Vatican said previously that Leo was expected to spend about a week recovering in the hospital after the surgery, and that all audiences with the pope were canceled until Oct. 20.

The pope, 71, announced during his weekly blessing and prayer in St. Peter’s Square on Sunday that doctors had advised the surgical intervention after detecting a “very early-stage and well-localized” nodule during recent medical tests.

Pulmonary nodules are very common, and most are benign, according to the American Lung Association.

Dr. Marco Alloisio, a thoracic surgeon at the Humanitas Cancer Center in Milan, emphasized that “a pulmonary nodule isn’t necessarily synonymous with lung cancer.”

He said that any further treatment would depend on the histological examination of the nodule and other biological tests that would check for genetic mutations. Dr. Alloisio, who is not part of the pope’s care, called it “very positive” that Leo had been receiving checkups.

Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer deaths in the United States, and older adults are at higher risk. Annual screening has been shown to save lives.

Dr. Lorenzo Spaggiari, a thoracic surgical oncologist at the European Institute of Oncology in Milan who is also not part of the pope’s medical team, said the pope’s surgery was likely to be minimally invasive, using robotic surgical procedures. A biopsy of the nodule would determine whether it needed to be removed and, if so, what percentage of the pulmonary lobe along with it.

While hospitalized, the pope is expected to remain in charge at the Vatican unless he is incapacitated, but day-to-day decisions are to be handled by its sprawling bureaucracy. Any major decision requiring papal approval is expected to be postponed until his release.

The pope had been scheduled to preside on Wednesday over the concluding Mass for a Vatican meeting about how a document on marriage and the family has been followed in the 10 years since it was issued.

Instead, the Mass will be presided over by Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle, 69, who was approved by Leo last week as the new dean of the College of Cardinals. The dean, who coordinates the activities of his fellow cardinals, plays an important role during any papal transition.

However, Leo appeared optimistic that he would be on his feet soon. He is scheduled to travel to South America early next month, a homecoming of sorts given that he worked and lived in Peru for many years. In his remarks last Sunday, Leo suggested he was still planning to go.

Dr. Spaggiari said that after lung surgery, patients are advised not to travel by plane for three weeks.

Asked whether the trip, which is to begin on Nov. 6, was still on the pope’s schedule, Matteo Bruni, the Vatican spokesman, said Tuesday morning that the pope had said it was.

item.title: FIFA’s Trump Tower Deal: 7 Years, $4 Million, One Mostly Unused Office
item.description:
About a year before the World Cup, FIFA held a splashy opening for its latest office, a 17th-floor suite in Trump Tower. President Trump’s son Eric Trump said his family’s organization was “honored” to host the global soccer body.

FIFA signed a more than seven-year lease, worth about $4 million, according to two officials directly involved in the deal and documents reviewed by The New York Times. The suite mostly sits empty.

The terms of the deal, which have not been previously reported, raised concern among some senior FIFA officials about renting space in a Trump-linked building, in a high-tax state, without a clear need.

The deal offers another example of how FIFA and its president, Gianni Infantino, sought closer ties to President Trump ahead of the 2026 World Cup, despite pushback from senior soccer officials.

Mr. Infantino has lavished praise on the American president, even creating a special peace prize in his honor. During the World Cup, FIFA rescinded the suspension of Folarin Balogun, a star striker for the U.S. team, after a call between Mr. Trump and Mr. Infantino, prompting accusations of bias and political interference.

Since the tournament, Mr. Infantino has faced intense scrutiny over his conduct, including for engaging in secret talks to sell a portion of future tournaments to a private fund run by the brother of Mr. Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner. The plan prompted European soccer’s governing body to threaten to bring a complaint to criminal court. Mr. Infantino has accused his critics of a harassment campaign.

FIFA’s American operations are mostly based in two offices in Miami. The organization has no plans to fully staff the Trump Tower location and the office sits largely idle, according to current and former FIFA officials who, like others cited in this article, requested anonymity to discuss private discussions and business deals.

The White House declined to comment. The Trump Organization did not respond to a request for comment.

In response to questions about the lease, FIFA defended the arrangement, saying that it paid market-level rent for the property. The lease “complies with all local laws” and “was signed in accordance with FIFA’s standard internal processes,” FIFA said in a statement.

FIFA uses the nearly 5,000-square-foot space for special events and for meetings with dignitaries and soccer leaders, the organization said. It is mostly used during the yearly United Nations General Assembly.

The decision to open a representative office in Trump Tower was driven by Mr. Infantino, according to the two officials who were involved in the deal.

FIFA hired an international real estate consultancy to assess whether the deal was in line with market rates. But the two officials said that there was no clear business need for the office, especially since FIFA had the offices in Miami.

Officials flagged that opening another U.S. office, in New York State, could create an additional tax liability for FIFA, the documents show, and the organization worked with lawyers to establish that no business or commercial activities would take place there to avoid such taxes.

In an emailed response to questions about the lease, FIFA said, “New York is a global city, and FIFA is a global organization; it is therefore logical for FIFA to have a presence there.”

Miguel Maduro, a Portuguese former governance head at FIFA, said that selecting a facility tied to the American president might breach the organization’s conflict-of-interest provisions.

“This deal with the Trump Organization raises a clear conflict of interest in the light of FIFA’s interests in the U.S. World Cup or its partnership with President Trump’s Board of Peace,” Mr. Maduro said. As part of the plan, FIFA in February announced a proposal to build fields and a stadium in Gaza.

Mr. Infantino’s relationship with Mr. Trump has also prompted an ethics complaint by Norway’s soccer federation.

Alex Phillips, a former official at FIFA and other top soccer governing bodies, called the Trump Tower office “a completely unnecessary level of pandering.”

]]>

item.title: U.K. and Europe Recoil From Trump’s Diesel Deal With Putin
item.description:
European and British officials were stunned by President Trump’s unexpected announcement that he had made a deal with President Vladimir V. Putin to purchase Russian diesel fuel. But they were in a bind on how to respond.

The arrangement, which President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine called “a gift” to President Putin, directly undercuts years of effort by dozens of countries — including the United States — to cut Russia off from the money that fuels Mr. Putin’s war of aggression in Ukraine.

Energy experts have said that the diesel agreement, if it goes ahead, could send some $4 billion of American money into the Russian economy.

Mr. Trump’s announcement on Friday afternoon of his “highly successful discussion” with Mr. Putin was all the more shocking in Europe as it came after Russia conducted several brutal strikes in Ukraine, killing 22 people including three babies in an apartment block on Wednesday and at least 30 people in a bus on Thursday.

For European leaders, the dilemma over the past three days has been familiar: How to support Ukraine in a moment of acute diplomatic peril, without triggering Mr. Trump’s ire?

As they scrambled for a response, they have stopped short of directly criticizing the American president and coalesced around a single diplomatic message: We are not changing our own approach to Russia, and we stand by Ukraine.

On Saturday, Britain announced that Prime Minister Andy Burnham had spoken to Mr. Zelensky, noting that he had begun the call “by recognizing the last 24 hours had been difficult for Ukraine” — an oblique reference to Mr. Trump’s intervention — and had “reiterated his complete solidarity.” The statement added that Mr. Burnham would meet with Mr. Zelensky in the coming days.

A spokesman for the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, told reporters that the government was “standing by the sanctions decisions against Russia and is working together with its European partners on further sanctions.”

Kaja Kallas, the European Union’s top diplomat, began her comments to reporters on Monday with a conciliatory nod to the United States, before saying that the bloc was “continuing our path” of trying to keep Russia from enriching itself by blocking the sale of oil and gas on the global market.

“The U.S. is our biggest ally, but our message is clear,” she said while entering a meeting of foreign affairs ministers in Luxembourg. “If we want to end this war, the only way we can do this is by putting more pressure on Russia.”

Margus Tsahkna, the minister of foreign affairs for Estonia, was more blunt.

“We have had this kind of turbulence and also pressure from President Trump’s side to Ukraine before,” he said. “So we need to focus on what we can do.”

Mr. Trump responded to the European reaction on his TruthSocial site Monday afternoon.

“The European Union paid Russia 250 Billion Dollars for Energy, and the Fake News Media doesn’t want to get near that story,” the president wrote, possibly referring to European purchases of Russian oil since Russia invaded. “I made the right choice for the American People — ALWAYS, AMERICA FIRST!”

It is true that the European Union continues to buy Russian energy, though the bloc has been working to wean itself off it and has sharply reduced its dependence.

Since beginning his second term, Mr. Trump has repeatedly indicated support for Russia’s positions over those of Ukraine. Before his re-election, the president promised to end the war in 24 hours and has on several occasions blamed Mr. Zelensky for the continued fighting.

“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal, because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does,” Mr. Trump said Saturday.

On Sunday, the president announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an “ENERGY CEASEFIRE,” though neither side confirmed that such an agreement existed. Several European leaders on Monday welcomed such a cease-fire but noted that Russia struck Ukrainian energy facilities after the announcement.

For European officials, the latest example of the president’s go-it-alone diplomacy with Mr. Putin strikes at the heart of their attempts to maintain a consensus on opposing Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Nearly three dozen countries, including Britain, France and Germany, formed what they called the “coalition of the willing” last year to demonstrate their resolve in supporting Ukraine.

None of the countries want to engage in a direct military confrontation with Russia. Instead, they have focused on helping Ukraine acquire weapons to defend itself. And they have used economic sanctions designed to cut Russia off from its most lucrative exports.

On Monday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk of Poland urged the United States and other European nations to increase sanctions — not back away from them.

“This message must go out today from every capital, from Warsaw to Washington,” he said. “I am certain that our response in the coming hours, weeks and months will be one of full solidarity and determination on the part of the free world, all capitals and all political leaders.”

He added, in words that signaled a more complicated reality: “I very much hope so.”

]]>

item.title: The Oct. 7 Attack Changed Israel, but Not Its Politics
item.description:
For one day last week, much of Israel united to commemorate the anniversary of the deadliest attack in the country’s history.

But when Israelis head to the ballot box this month, they will be carrying sharply disparate versions of who is to blame for failing to prevent the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led assault. Though the attack traumatized Israel, it did not produce the kind of rage that would create a political transformation, leaving the country more polarized than ever.

The political divide is nowhere clearer than among the Israelis living closest to the Gaza border, where thousands of gunmen overran communities, army bases and a music festival.

In Nahal Oz, a pastoral kibbutz half a mile from the border, the gardens are blooming again with the return of residents evacuated during the war. Many in this liberal bastion are likely to vote against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his hawkish policies, holding him responsible for failures leading to Oct. 7, said Daniel Rahamim, 72, a spokesman for the community, who survived the assault along with his family.

“We don’t have the privilege of giving up on peace,” he said.

Barely eight miles away in the working-class town of Sderot, the scene of a fierce firefight during the Hamas-led attack, Mr. Netanyahu remains a hero. In the view of many residents, he was let down — or even betrayed — by his security chiefs in the run-up to Oct. 7 and on the day of the assault.

“If the left wins, we’re done for, it will be the end of Israel,” said Shlomi Aragon, 55, referring to anybody critical of Mr. Netanyahu.

The election, set for Oct. 27, will be the first since Hamas militants and their allies surged across the border from Gaza, killing about 1,200 people, mostly civilians, according to the Israeli authorities, and taking 251 hostages.

Israel’s devastating war in response reduced much of the Palestinian enclave to rubble and left more than 74,000 people dead, including thousands of children, according to Gaza health officials, who do not distinguish between civilians and combatants.

Many Israelis view this month’s vote as the most momentous since their country’s establishment nearly eight decades ago, and for reasons that are not limited to Oct. 7. Mr. Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition, Israel’s most hard-line and religiously conservative, has undermined the country’s democratic foundations, critics say, and left it diplomatically isolated.

Hanging over the election most intensely are questions about the missteps in the prelude to Oct. 7 — for the policies aimed at fostering quiet in Hamas-run Gaza in the years before the attack and for military and intelligence lapses that left Israel vulnerable. These failures have profoundly shaken people’s confidence in the state’s ability to protect them.

The wars that spread from Gaza to Lebanon and Iran in the aftermath of the Oct. 7 attack remain unfinished. Three years on, Israel’s enemies are battered but not out, defying Mr. Netanyahu’s promises of total victory.

Yet all this upheaval has not produced the radical shift that would upend Israel’s politics.

“Like everyone, after Oct. 7, I thought there would be an earthquake,” said Tamar Hermann, a professor of political science and expert in public opinion at the Israel Democracy Institute, a nonpartisan research group in Jerusalem.

Instead, she said, it has reinforced people’s previously held positions as they retreated to their political “comfort zones.”

Like past elections, this one, too, revolves largely around the question of “Yes Bibi or no Bibi,” Ms. Hermann said, using Mr. Netanyahu’s nickname, and the choice between a “more Jewish or more democratic” Israel.

The Netanyahu camp, for its part, says Israel’s security services failed to respond to the grave threat posed by Hamas, not the prime minister or the policies of his ruling Likud party.

There is little argument among most Israelis over the government’s new willingness to carry out sustained attacks beyond the country’s borders and occupy territory in Gaza, Syria and Lebanon. A majority of Israelis fear a repeat of Oct. 7, according to a recent survey by the Institute for National Security Studies at Tel Aviv University.

But that view does not extend to confidence in Mr. Netanyahu’s leadership. Surveys indicate a split electorate and a typically tight race with a high likelihood that neither Mr. Netanyahu, Israel’s longest serving prime minister, nor his chief rival, Gadi Eisenkot, a centrist and former military chief, will secure an easy path toward forming the next government.

On the Israeli side of the Gaza border, the air of renewal masks sharp disagreements over the lessons of Oct. 7.

During the attack, 15 people in Nahal Oz were killed, and eight residents were kidnapped, including one who died in captivity. Most of the residents have since returned to the kibbutz. At night, the lights of Israeli army positions visible along a ridge inside the Gaza Strip provide some sense of security.

Mr. Rahamim, the Nahal Oz spokesman, has a fresh tattoo on his arm bearing the date of the attack and the words, “On the path of hope.” The image of a sunflower climbing his forearm symbolizes a local crop — and hope, Mr. Rahamim said, “because it always faces the sun.”

In the last national election, held in 2022, 83 percent of the voters in Nahal Oz supported centrist and left-leaning parties. In the upcoming election, Mr. Rahamim said he and many neighbors will likely vote against Mr. Netanyahu again.

Mr. Netanyahu’s handling of Gaza is not the only reason. Mr. Rahamim also pointed to the government’s efforts at curbing the powers of the judiciary and at the influence Mr. Netanyahu’s ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies have over him, leading Mr. Rahamim to ask, “Will Israel be a liberal democratic state or gradually turn into a religious or fascist state?”

Some attitudes have hardened here, too, since the Oct. 7 attack. “If there is a consensus here in community, it is that Hamas has to be destroyed,” Mr. Rahamim said.

Unlike many in Mr. Netanyahu’s camp, Mr. Rahamim also said he believes that Israel must eventually negotiate an accommodation with moderate Palestinian leaders. “We have an obligation to our grandchildren,” he said.

In Sderot, forests of construction cranes rise from new neighborhoods. A serene memorial park has replaced the police station where a deadly battle raged. More than 50 people were killed in the city, including civilians, police officers, firefighters and soldiers.

Sderot has historically been a stronghold of Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party, and in the last election, 79 percent voted for the right-wing and strictly Orthodox parties that made up his governing coalition.

Here, residents espouse conspiracy theories spread by Mr. Netanyahu’s camp that treasonous generals and security chiefs kept the prime minister in the dark about the start of the Hamas attack.

Mr. Netanyahu has asserted that Israeli security officials had chosen not to awaken him in the early hours of Oct. 7, despite worrying signs from Gaza.. He has blocked the establishment of an independent inquiry into what went wrong, despite a strong public demand for one.

Mr. Aragon, who owns a shawarma restaurant, said he narrowly escaped death on Oct. 7 when gunmen drove behind him and started shooting. About 20 years ago, he said, his house was hit by a rocket from Gaza that severely injured his wife.

He described Mr. Netanyahu as “the war leader of a generation” and suggested that the Israeli air force, if activated, could have halted the Hamas invasion within an hour. “There was a betrayal. It’ll come out,” he said.

Living opposite the site of the destroyed police station, Evelyn Sayada, 60, whose son-in-law survived the assault on the music festival, said she felt constant anxiety because Hamas had not been disarmed. But she said she would almost certainly vote for Mr. Netanyahu, as her family has always done.

“I don’t think he failed,” she said. “There was treason.”

One of the worst-hit Israeli border villages was Kfar Aza, home to Yonatan Shamriz, 36. His brother, Alon, was taken hostage and later killed accidentally by Israeli soldiers in Gaza who had mistaken him and two other captives for militants.

Mr. Shamriz emerged from a life of relative obscurity and founded a grass-roots movement to cultivate new leadership and change called “Kumu!” — Hebrew for “awaken!” or “rise up!”

Faced with what they call government efforts to blur and forget, he and Kumu organized Israel’s main Oct. 7 memorial ceremony for the last three years, embracing families of victims from across Israeli society — left and right-wingers, religious and secular, Jews and Arabs. Tens of thousands attended this year’s memorial, and Israel’s leading television channels aired it live.

Mr. Shamriz now lives far from the Gaza border, in a trailer with his wife and three young children in a kibbutz on the coast north of Tel Aviv. He said he believes another attack like the one on Oct. 7 is a matter of time. “If not next year, then in 10 years,” he said.

Last year, Mr. Shamriz announced that he was entering politics, aiming to create a new, unifying force with a vision based on the lessons of Oct. 7. “Something young and fresh,” he said.

In September, he quit, concluding that Israelis weren’t ready to leave their old politics behind.

“For now, people are afraid of change,” he said. “Everyone wants to vote for an experienced politician or general — someone they know.”

]]>
